q: Rotenone blocks complex I. Isolated mitochondria with rotenone can still make some ATP if given succinate. Why?
options: Succinate is converted straight into ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation inside the matrix
Rotenone only inhibits ATP synthase, so electrons can still flow along the entire chain to O2
Succinate's electrons enter at complex II, past the block, so complexes III and IV still pump H+
Succinate supplies extra O2 to complex IV, which restarts electron flow from the stalled NADH
explanation: Rotenone stops NADH's electrons entering at complex I. Electrons from succinate enter at complex II (succinate dehydrogenase → FADH2 → ubiquinone), downstream of the block, so electron flow through complexes III and IV – and proton pumping – continues, giving ~1.5 ATP per succinate oxidised. This shows NADH and FADH2 feed electrons in at different points.
